title: Optimal one-pass randomized space for LIS length
formal:
Determine, up to constant factors, the optimal randomized one-pass streaming space in bits for a factor-two estimate of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of a length-\(n\) sequence over \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

For every fixed input \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}^n\), let
\[L(x)=\max\{r:\exists\,1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le n,\ x_{i_1}<\cdots<x_{i_r}\}.\]
An admissible algorithm reads \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) once in this order and, after the final item, outputs an integer \(\widehat L\) such that
\[\Pr\bigl[L(x)/2\le\widehat L\le L(x)\bigr]\ge2/3.\]
Find an explicit asymptotic function \(f(n)\) admitting a uniform algorithm with \(O(f(n))\) worst-case bit space and a matching \(\Omega(f(n))\) lower bound for every admissible randomized algorithm. Logarithmic factors are part of the requested answer.
why: This problem tests whether randomness can substantially reduce the memory needed to retain ordered structure in a sequence. The large gap between what is known for deterministic algorithms and what is proved necessary for ordinary randomized algorithms makes it a basic unresolved question about one-pass computation.
status_note: Source-open in Sublinear.info Problem 44, Bertinoro 2011, updated 7 March 2013. The selected version uses one pass over length-n sequences from {1,...,n}, a factor-two underestimate and success at least 2/3. On 16 September 2026 the review checked the SODA 2007 upper bound, Chakrabarti’s 2010/2012 communication result and the published ITCS 2026 paper, whose introduction explicitly leaves ordinary randomized LIS approximation open. Its Theorem 1 is a white-box adversarial result for factor 1.1 and alphabet size at least 3n, so it does not resolve the selected model. A bounded later-work search found no verified matching randomized bounds; this does not certify the entire literature or supply a Lean proof.

progress.text: A deterministic one-pass approximation uses \(O(\sqrt n\log(n+2))\) bits for the selected alphabet and fixed accuracy, giving a valid randomized upper bound.

Chakrabarti proves that the communication problems behind earlier deterministic lower bounds have efficient randomized protocols. Those reductions therefore do not yield matching randomized lower bounds.

Gal, Kol, Saxena and Yu prove a square-root white-box lower bound with the additional model and accuracy conditions stated above; they still describe ordinary randomized LIS approximation as a longstanding open problem.

importance.reason: A longstanding central streaming problem with a substantial unresolved benefit-of-randomness question. The fixed one-pass model and finite alphabet make a matching bit-space determination precise while retaining the main conceptual difficulty.

sentences: The problem asks for optimal bit space to estimate the longest strictly increasing subsequence in one streaming pass.
Inputs are arbitrary length-n sequences of numbers from one to n, fixed before the algorithm chooses its random bits.
The final estimate must lie between half the true length and the true length with probability at least two thirds.
Deterministic upper bounds and recent lower bounds against a stronger adaptive adversary leave the ordinary randomized optimum unresolved.
The requested answer must match upper and lower bounds up to constants, including every logarithmic factor.

definitions:
The stream length \(n\ge1\) is known before the stream begins. The input contains exactly \(n\) integers, each in the ordered alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), represented in binary. Repetitions are allowed: the input is an arbitrary sequence and need not be a permutation. The asymptotic parameter is the number of items \(n\), whereas memory is measured in bits, not in stored items or machine words. An explicit input list occupies \(O(n\log(n+2))\) bits.

An increasing subsequence retains selected positions in their original order; the positions need not be consecutive. Both inequalities in its definition are strict. In particular, repeated equal values cannot both appear in such a subsequence. The strictly decreasing sequence has LIS length one, while \((1,2,\ldots,n)\) has LIS length \(n\). The problem asks only for the length estimate. It does not require the positions or values of a witnessing subsequence.

A single pass gives sequential access to the items from first to last, with no rewind, rereading, permutation of the stream or random-access queries to earlier positions. The algorithm may retain information about previous items only in its working memory. Its output appears after the whole sequence has been processed. It need not approximate the LIS of every prefix or issue intermediate answers.

For each fixed valid sequence, the probability is taken over independent fair random bits used by the algorithm. The entire input is fixed independently of those bits. The guarantee is required separately for every sequence, including sequences with short LIS; there is no promise that the LIS contains a constant fraction of the input. The algorithm may fail on at most one third of its random executions for a particular sequence. No distribution on input sequences is imposed.

The output convention is an underestimate within a factor two, as in the later paper's multiplicative approximation definition. On successful executions it lies in \([L(x)/2,L(x)]\). This is not the wider interval \([L(x)/2,2L(x)]\). The output can be an integer: rounding up a real output in the chosen interval preserves both bounds because \(L(x)\) is an integer. No additive error is allowed.

Use one finite uniform streaming program at all lengths. Its persistent state and temporary working storage are measured in bits; stored input values, counters, indices, retained random choices and output preparation all count. There is no external scratch storage, reusable random tape containing uncharged information, advice string or oracle. The stream itself is read-only sequential input. Fresh random bits may be consumed during computation; information about past bits can be reused only if it was retained within the counted memory.

Space is the maximum number of working bits used at any time, over every valid input of length \(n\) and every random execution, including executions whose final answer is inaccurate. Call this quantity \(s_A(n)\) for algorithm \(A\). It is not expected space. The algorithm must terminate after processing its input, but the target imposes no separate update-time or total-time bound. Unlimited local computation does not permit additional storage or another pass. Knowing \(n\) does not provide the input's LIS length or any statistic of the sequence.

The requested optimum means matching asymptotic upper and lower bounds in this model. There must be one admissible algorithm \(A_*\), a constant \(C>0\) and a threshold \(n_0\) with \(s_{A_*}(n)\le C f(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). For every admissible randomized algorithm \(A\), there must be constants \(c_A>0,n_A\) with \(s_A(n)\ge c_A f(n)\) for all \(n\ge n_A\). The constants are independent of the input and its random bits. The answer must state \(f\) explicitly and establish both directions; merely defining \(f\) to be the unknown optimum is not an answer.

All factors growing with \(n\), including \(\log n\), iterated logarithms or a slowly growing multiplier, must be retained. Determining only an exponent in \(n\), or proving bounds that match only after hiding logarithmic factors, does not meet the selected precision. No numerical additive tolerance applies to an asymptotic space bound.

The white-box adversarial model is different: its input generator may inspect the algorithm's previous random choices and internal memory before selecting the next item. A lower bound against algorithms required to survive that stronger input generator need not hold when the sequence is fixed beforehand. Deterministic algorithms, multiple-pass algorithms, algorithms with reordered access and additive approximations are also separately specified variants. The original source mentions both one and constantly many passes; the user selected exactly one pass and the alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
answer_criterion: Give an explicit function \(f(n)\) and complete Lean-checked proofs of the matching uniform upper and randomized lower space bounds defined above. The algorithm must meet the factor-two interval and success probability on every fixed input, using one pass and counted worst-case bit space. The lower bound must apply to randomized algorithms in this same fixed-input model and alphabet, not only to deterministic or white-box adversarial algorithms. A single improved bound without a matching other direction, an additive approximation, an algorithm for a larger approximation factor or bounds differing by a logarithmic factor do not complete the selected constant-factor determination.

source_formulation.text: Chakrabarti asks for the randomized streaming space complexity of a factor-two LIS-length approximation and mentions both one pass and a constant number of passes. The user selected one pass, length-n sequences over the alphabet {1,…,n}, success probability at least two thirds and optimal bit space up to constant factors. The strict-increase convention and the multiplicative output interval are stated explicitly.

context_blocks.text: The length of the longest increasing subsequence measures how much ordered structure survives inside a sequence. Computing or estimating it differs from sorting: only a number is requested, yet information from distant positions can determine which choices combine into a long subsequence.

Gopalan and coauthors give a deterministic one-pass approximation algorithm using \(O(\sqrt n)\) stored input symbols for fixed relative accuracy. With alphabet \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the corresponding bit bound is \(O(\sqrt n\log(n+2))\). Their discussion explains how to handle strict rather than nondecreasing subsequences. This is an upper bound for randomized algorithms as well, because they may ignore randomness.

Deterministic lower bounds leave open whether randomness saves substantially more memory. Chakrabarti shows that the communication problems used in those lower bounds admit inexpensive randomized protocols. This establishes a limitation of those particular lower-bound arguments; it does not provide a small-space randomized LIS algorithm.

The ITCS 2026 paper proves a square-root space lower bound in the white-box model for a 1.1-approximation with an alphabet of size at least three times the stream length. Its theorem differs from this card in the adversary, accuracy and stated alphabet. Its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary randomized approximation problem as open.

An additive approximation to LIS length can be useful when \(L(x)\) is large. An additive error proportional to \(n\), however, can exceed the entire answer when \(L(x)\ll n\). Likewise, an approximation to the complementary quantity \(n-L(x)\), the number of deletions needed to leave a strictly increasing sequence, need not approximate a small \(L(x)\) multiplicatively.

This is an unusual streaming question in which a sublinear-space deterministic algorithm is known but the benefit of randomness remains poorly understood. Matching randomized bounds would explain whether the memory cost comes from the ordered structure of the input or from limitations of deterministic summaries.
